video_title: Stripe’s John Collison: AI Agents Will Rewire the Internet
transcript: Please join me in welcoming to the stage Molly O'Shea and John Collison. >> John, thank you very much. And Paul, thank you very much. I hope you guys are all having a really great day. Um, enjoying everything browserbased. So, we're going to talk about payments, Aenta Commerce, and everything that's going on in the computer. So, Stripe processed $1.9 trillion dollar in 2025, up 34%. >> How how are you rebuilding for AI? >> Yeah, look, it's really interesting right now because we've been working on Stripe for a long time, right? We've been This is our 17th year doing it. And for many years in the payments industry, didn't really change that much. And now there's just like some small changes happening where I mean leave aside everything that's going on in stable coins and like all that other interesting stuff but other than that it's all same old. >> So instinct is real, muse is real. >> All these things are real. Again you have people in the a like you've you saw a significant fraction of the audience uh using them and okay I think it turns out one filling out a web form is not a value ad activity for anyone. like no one chooses to fill out web forms in their spare time. Uh and so I think the whole conceit of these agents and obviously again this is where um browserbased and you know computer use comes in but when you have the stateful context where your agent knows things about you like the basic one is it knows your shipping address and payment details and things like that and then when it can manipulate a computer and go off and do things in the real world it turns out it's much nicer to be able to say hey please renew my driver's license for me or you know whatever the task is rather than go play with uh with web forms. And so I actually think um one big part of all these personal agents starting to work is actually giving them a meaningful amount of compute uh so you can go do stuff. But another one is computer use actually becoming a mature enough technology because computer use is the ultimate backwards compatibility layer for the real world. Like how long would you need to wait for, you know, the DMV to add an MCP? Like I I'm not a betting man, but I'm betting we would have to wait a few years, but it doesn't matter because computer use solves that. And so again, it's the ultimate backwards compatibility there. >> So you've mentioned that Agentic Commerce is a complete rewiring. What do you mean by it's complete rewiring? >> A few things. One is like it's rewiring things at the surface level where uh how businesses sell is going to change pretty um significantly. Like the first order change is that we think people's agents are going to be uh doing a huge amount of the commerce for them. The second change is maybe or the second order change is it probably changes the commerce landscape a little bit. And so again I don't know what people bought in their experiences but my experience of doing AI powered product research is it often actually surfaces niche brands or businesses you haven't heard of. Like I think it's quite a good story for the long tale of businesses. I think it's quite empowering that if you have a product that actually is well reviewed and that you know people like on the internet, it leads to more discovery of that. And so I think the existing aggregators are going to have to answer questions because in a way AI discovery is the new point of aggregation for commerce. And so you probably have a bit of a turning over of the top businesses. That's going to happen where if you are selling a really good product, if you're making it discoverable, then you can kind of shoot up in the rankings. I think the analogy for this is when like Facebook and Instagram ad targeting was so good that it led to a whole new generation of companies that were built around, you know, targeting on those platforms and they were native to it. think of a Wish.com or a Teespring or uh you know even Timu and Shien in you know to a significant degree grew up on those platforms and did a huge amount of customer acquisition on those platforms and they were able to more natively adopt it than the prior generation of big box retailers who in theory had all the same tools available to them but they were just less native to that kind of customer acquisition technology and it you know it's got to flow all the way downstream to the product creation and things like that. I feel like AI e-commerce will be somewhat similar where first order it'll make buying things more convenient. Second order it'll probably actually reshape the product and the merchant landscape uh to be to favor the people who can most successfully adopt it. >> Well, how are you thinking about cyber security risk as that scales? We have invented a new technology that is uh available to defenders and available to attackers. And you know people make all the you know trit um analogies to um you know the the emergence of the motorc car you know the uh bank robbers uh were the first to adopt the car uh uh to conduct bank robberies and pretty quickly you know police forces started realizing hm we really need cars to keep up with these bank robbers. H and so you always have this like cat and mouse offense uh defense game that's happening. Uh and so in our case, the new models have really advanced cyber capabilities and it's I mean somewhat intimidating because you're realizing that the standard for I mean the good news is that Stripe has been very paranoid on cyber for many many years and so it's not like this is kind of totally new news for us but we feel like the adversary landscape is getting quite a bit better quite quickly and so it went from something that we already had a ton of attention on to something that we're spending even more attention on and it does feel like over say over the next five years you're going to see more breaches than you did over the past five years. >> Dark. [snorts] >> This is true. Like there's no two ways about it because again in theory there should be some equilibrium between offense and defense but that's this very like assume a spherical cow theory and in practice there are lots of organizations out there that are going to be too slow in how they adopt the latest capabilities. The good news for like the startups in the room is obviously I think startups are um disproportionately in a good spot because it is easier for them to adopt the latest models with kind of the latest cyber capabilities and they just have smaller more contained more homogeneous tech stacks versus if you're running some like 50-year-old tech stack that has grown through acquisition where you have like a bunch of you know you're running on versions of Windows that aren't even supported anymore like that's not a great place to from a cyber point of view. >> So you've talked about Singularity a bunch. You have a different perspective on it that I think is like a little bit more optimistic than the standard San Francisco Doom. So [snorts] how do you I guess what is your perspective on Singularity? How do you make this? >> Yeah, you know, we've been um we kind of somewhat uh tongue and cheek at Stripe started referring to January 1st as uh you know, day one of the singularity. And so kind of like the Unix epoch is um you know January 1st 1970 which decided that um the uh the singularity epoch is January 1st 2026. That's a good a day as any to decide that you know we are now in the in the singularity. And I mean it's not a total coincidence that we picked that date in that if you guys remember it was the end of last year that I feel like for many of us it was the holy crap moment when it came to coding models and how they're getting that good how they're getting so good and in particular you know the thing that they all the AI folks talk about is this idea of recursive self-improvement where you know the AI uses um the AI to make itself better. And again, I think sometimes it uh it's a bit challenging because people refer to the the AI as kind of this monolithic thing, but we're clearly in a world where AI capabilities are helping with the rate of improvement in AI. I mean, just look at all the math announcements that we had um this week and last week. We're in math wars now. Um it's just it's not something that was on my bingo card for uh for 2026 that we have math wars. Um but uh you know rival mass factions um but we have and kind of the same thing applies to the uh the model development where the labs are using AI capabilities to uh to go faster. So anyway, it feels like 2026 is this year where we're really feeling the effects of that recursive self-improvement. I think we're pretty optimistic at Stripe. Like we see we see the early economic indicators from this where as a result of intelligence on tap getting much cheaper, new firm creation is way up. We're seeing the highest rate of um of new firm creation that we've seen in recent memory on Stripe like right now because when you have all these tools, it's easier to start a company. It's easier to actually make it successful. Um I I think this this technology has a lot to be optimistic about and so we don't say the singularity in um any kind of a uh pessimistic or kind of worried manner. It's just like we are in this moment of AI takeoff right now and you should enjoy it and it's kind of hard to deny that it's happening. >> Should we be scared or is that just marketing tactic? [sighs] in a business context. Firstly, I think you should be paying attention. Like the thing that we tell businesses, you know, that we're working with at Stripe is, you know, when we're talking about this cyber stuff, all the cyber stuff is real. And again, just as we're talking about the agent commerce stuff earlier, the entire landscape is shifting. I'll give you another example. We spent, you know, again, the entirety of Stripe up to this point, building for developers and using APIs as a selling point, like making the developer experience easy was um what we focused on, what we spent a huge amount of internal effort on at Stripe. And this would be like minute details of the API documentation or how we make upgrades easy for a developer who's migrating from, you know, one version of the API to the other overnight, you know, relatively overnight. No one actually really integrates the Stripe API by hand anymore. You know, they send their coding agent to do it. And that's a related skill, but it's actually a pretty different skill because uh you know the developer ergonomics are different from the AI ergonomics. And so many of the things that we spend time on to make things nice for developers actually don't really matter to the AIS and what matters is a fairly different set of things like it's very easy for them to uh you know integrate the wrong version of the API or something like this. And so we are having to kind of totally change what we're good at internally at Stripe. I think that's probably true for all the industries people are working in here where just everyone's chessboard just got a little bit of a jiggle and some of the pieces got knocked and you know the position moved around and so now you're working with this uh this new chess position. I think everyone needs to um pay advantage to that. I think one should worry about specific concerns and so you should like specifically feel good about your cyber security or ensure that you can uh feel good about it. I don't think people should feel this like ominous oppressive overbearing sense of foroding generally I think they should feel pretty excited to be living in this fast takeoff world. >> So Stripe is taking off even faster than before. uh you have most recently made a couple of really interesting acquisitions from metronome bridge privy to also open router. So what are you assembling there? How are you redirecting for this era? >> So if you look at the areas where stripe has done acquisitions they tend to follow that pattern where bridge and privy were in crypto and again there is a certain kind of cryptonativity and way of working in the crypto world that is different to the world that we came from. And so the folks on those teams are cryptonative in a way that it would be hard to get there that quickly at Stripe and they've injected a lot of that crypto nativity in the stripe culture. You know, you mentioned metronome which is usagebased spelling because of AI. Everyone has inference costs these days and so everyone has to uh actually price their product differently. There are very few products these days that do not have some usage based component or some overage. like you can sign up for chat or claude and they will let you go a certain amount but then they're like sorry you ran out of plan you got to buy credits and so because of the underlying cost structure kind of everyone needs to have usage based billing these days um uh with AI products and then you mentioned open router we're just well one I think we're obviously um pretty AI build like uh like everyone else in the audience and what we notice is that a huge fraction of an increasing fraction and increasingly a huge fraction of businesses spend is actually going towards just AI and inference and that could be you know you're doing R&D at your company or a lot of products actually have some AI inference as part of delivering the product and you could say oh we're iterating towards you know the single model that everyone will use for everything I think open router's belief is that like to believe in open router you have to believe that more than one model will be used inside a business like the same business uh and maybe that that model will change and so people might want to depending on the particular workload send things to a different model. They may want to update that when new better models come out. They may want to when you think about it a really high value user you can send to a frontier model but a lower value user you write to a lower value model and so it depends on your you the user is lifetime value to you all this kind of stuff. But if you believe that you actually just need to use multiple models at the same time within a business, then you need something like Open Router. And as far as we could tell, they were the furthest ahead in delivering that marketplace to help businesses actually use multiple models. >> So Stripe's goal is to increase the GDP of the internet. How much of this is coming from AI now? >> Like I won't say the exact fraction, but a lot. Uh and part of the reason I won't say the exact like partly because I don't want to um but partly um because it's actually pretty hard to measure these days where uh there's are you know AI business you know the browser bases of the world running on Stripe clearly you know at the core of the AI revolution you know allowing people to actually you know allowing agents to actually use computers that's pretty clearly in the AI category there's a lot of businesses out there that are transforming their business with AI. They they grew up in the pre-AII, you know, Meta runs on Stripe, grew up in the pre-AI era, pretty increasingly becoming an AI company. And so we find it very hard to segment companies into, you know, AI versus not AI because if you're not using a lot of AI in your business, you're probably not paying attention. >> In terms of acquisitions and strategic thinking about the business and growth and new products that you're offering, when do you decide to build versus buy? That is one of the, you know, in the early days of Stripe, I, you know, would go meet with the leaders of, um, much larger and kind of further ahead companies and ask them questions like that and pretty quick. I remember asking um, uh, you know, actually I remember asking uh, Aaron Levy of Box at one point, asking how product prioritization should work and he was like, "Yeah, you make a big list of all the product things you want to do and then you do the things that'll be most impactful." uh and they're like thanks okay it sounds very actionable but it's a little bit like that on the build versus buy where you should um you should buy the companies where you're better off buying them than building it in-house uh it's that is where I think all the the taste and and nuance is I think we have tended to buy in the past when it is a something that's like really in the core stripe we're probably more likely to be good at doing it ourselves uh whereas something that is a brand new muscle like token routing. I trust that Stripe could you know learn to get good at that but it would take much longer. And then the question is how fast is the market evolving and I mean open routers market is totally different today than it was 12 months ago and it's going to be totally different again 12 months in the future. And so I think that combination of like a new and really fast evolving market often time by the time you build your internal effort it'll be a little bit out of date or something. >> What have been the biggest transformations with AI internally at Stripe that you've been most excited about? Um you guys have all probably seen um or experienced the uh you know what they refer to as the jagged frontier the uneven performance of AI where it's really good in some domains and really bad in others. And for example if there is something where there is a huge corpus of data online then it probably does reasonably good of it. there's, you know, many areas where it doesn't have access to any training data and then, you know, suddenly it just kind of has to reason from first principles and it's much poorer. I think the organizational equivalent of that is like, yeah, you can do stuff in your random consumer AI app. That's not what you want to do in most business contexts. You want to actually ask it a question that has some um business context. And so, the reason I say this is we built our internal tool. I think a lot of companies have them, but it's been incredibly useful where you give the AI application access to the internal data with all the which is quite complex because you need to have all the privacy guardrails. You just need to have all the access control guardrails where like some people need to have access to the HR database but like everyone should not have access to the HR database and so uh the permissions gets pretty complex. uh just the correctness uh gets pretty complex but once you have that now you have an AI app internally that can work on the internal data sets and that becomes pretty powerful and for example all our sales teams I just completely changed their workflows where uh they can self-s serve all the stuff they need to you know if you want to have a personalized pitch uh for a customer they are building their AI applications to put together okay what is the data that will actually be of interest to this particular customer and again they're not using an application that we built for them they are building their own application and same with like okay the legal team give you an example they um people are almost writing new laws it turns out uh and you know we operate all around the world and so it's like oh this new like 600page law in India just dropped have you read it yet it's like sorry no I'm reading the 600page law that dropped in Finland and so they have a lot of stuff to keep up with and So uh someone on the legal team built their agent for ingesting all the new regulation that comes along that might be you know subject to strip. It's same with by the way computer use that's you know one of the reasons I am so excited about what companies like browser base are doing is because I feel like we're at this moment in time right now where computer use is finally getting good enough that it can actually be the next wave of AI progress like you think we had transformers and then using transformers we had LMS and then you know with LMS we added RL and there have been these kind of discrete hops of improvement in the development of AI uh over the years And my perspective at least is that good computer use is like will come to be viewed as one of these next hops because it is the backwards compatibility layer on the rest of the world. A and so I feel like that is going to be the next wave of AI applications is taking advantage of this new capability. How are you staying on top of all the research, all the new advancements? Um uh but I'm not sure they are either but um I vibe code my applications that I want to use and that's very enjoyable and again it's it's just you can actually get significant utility out of stuff um these days. Uh and then just constantly talk to Stripe customers about what they're doing. So we've always tried to uh you know look at where the puck is going rather than you know company's current scale and if you are spending time with the fast growing companies on the platform they will invariably be um be in AI or kind of around it in some way because that is just the fast growing area and so that also keeps me pretty fresh and stuff. >> Okay. [laughter] Um, what is more analog that helps me stay focused? Um, >> a favorite book, movies, normal human things. even all the normal human things like um uh getting out in nature like put putting down the phone from time to time. I don't know if people have tried that, but it's um it's pretty nice out there in the the wider world. Like, you know, we're here in California. It's like one of the nicest places in the world. And so, you just like go across the Golden Gate Bridge to Marin or something. And that's pretty pretty restorative pretty quickly. If people are visiting from out of town, you got to get like outside of Soma. So, if you're like coming to this conference and you're staying in Union Square or whatever, the key thing is you got to get outside of this one block radius, especially while Dreamforce is on. I mean, good god. A and so that is my main encouragement to it also will help with avoiding the uh the AI psychosis. >> I mean, it does surprise me because I visit here quite often. I don't live here that people come here as tourists. >> But it's beautiful. Of course they do. I know most places in the world. >> But like I'm just used to coming here and it's like an office park, you know, but people come here because of culture. >> Yeah. No, it's I don't know that that's a culture, but >> history. >> Yeah, [laughter] exactly. Nature. Yeah. Um, so what do you think, maybe this is a little bit more of a tricky question, but what do you think are the main or one of the questions that isn't being asked right now in this era, AI, agents, computer that we should be asking? Um well one like I said is I I think this is being asked but I think it's going to become a much louder and more pointed question is um for example many sites do bot detection and bot prevention and that is a reasonable thing to do or like it's understandable how they got there but like it's increasingly all bots and so what what is the new equivalent of um you know bot bot detection for the world we are going to where there is the you know there the good bots uh and then there are the bad bots and you need to be able to uh to to screen between them and so again I think we are just at this like this really interesting moment happening now where again as I see it you really should play with one of you know instinct or grockbot or um uh or uh muse uh from meta or any of these kind of uh AI assistant tools because they're a very powerful sense of uh what is coming uh and that new uh modality for how AI products will work. But again, I think they ask a lot of questions about what the new equilibrium will be and I think we just don't know that. >> As we close out, I have one last question, but over 17 years as a founder, what have been your biggest lessons? Look, I think if you're really looking to condense the Stripe story or or Stripe experience, one I'd say there's no shortcuts. Um, just Stripe never had a South by Southwest breakout moment. You know, there were times when, you know, be flicking the growth dial and saying, you know, is this thing on? Uh, and just it was growing. you just like every year has been a bigger year than the prior year and it turns out you just like do that enough years um one after another and you eventually get to 1.9 trillion but it never felt like oh my god this thing is really working it just felt like ah yeah I mean growth is down a bit from last year but like in absolute terms it's bigger and you uh you eventually get there and there's a lot of years of that and similarly like we'd invest everything I mean this is obviously kind of definitionally true every new product you start is kind of imit material and a toy to begin with, but we really rarely started products that felt like the future of the company at the time. We just started a neat thing that we thought delivered value for customers. Um, and so I think there's a real element of Stripe that is just stick withness where we didn't quit and we didn't get acquired and we just stayed plugging away at it. And I think that's underrated in a lot of um tech stories. Nvidia is the largest company in the world and they've just been making GPUs since the 1990s and they made better GPUs and again I think they thought of improvements like oh we should have CUDA and they you know they thought of these improvements to have but it's a real story of stickw with itness because there were many periods when Nvidia was much less hot uh than it is today. Um I think we always tried to play the long-term game you know infinite game with people um where you want to do right by your partners and you want to be seen as good to work with. I think reputation matters a lot. Uh, you know, we care about Stripe having a reputation for being a good company to work with. And so, uh, I think just treating being a good counterparty seriously or something is um, is something that really matters. And then the last one is uh, we talk about this at at Stripe. You know, our we have a set of operating principles in terms of how we work. Lots of business have them. Our first one is just users first and we always try to start with what does the customer actually want and work backwards from that especially when it comes to product development and I think it's very easy for companies to go a drift and start getting into you know you know what market we should get into or uh you know a great new revenue pool would be X or like really get into this internal company oriented way of thinking that's fine to do and you know people can like their spreadsheets or anything like that. Well, John Carlson, thank you so much and thank you to Paul and everyone at Browserbase and all of you for coming today.
